However, their reliability in structural engineering computations—where validity is highly sensitive to implementation details—remains insufficiently quantified. This study evaluates four recent reasoning-oriented LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeekV3.2, GPT5, and Grok 4 Fastreasoning) under a unified API-based setup with default parameters and proposes a novel evaluation framework tailored for structural simulation. Five problems are designed to cover linear elasticity problems, forced vibration of a Timoshenko beam, and frame analysis. Solution strategies are constrained for comparability, and all generated codes are executed in a fixed Python environment with results verified against ABAQUS simulations or analytical solutions. The framework explicitly probes the importance of boundary conditions, selection of modeling assumptions, and implementation robustness. Common failure modes include incorrect treatment of traction-free boundaries, local-to-global transformation errors due to inconsistent local-axis definitions, and numerical instability induced by the choices of ways to impose boundary conditions. Overall reliability shows GPT‐5 is best model among those models tested. These findings suggest that verification-oriented workflows and automated consistency checks are essential for the safe use of LLM-assisted structural computation.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6641752\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6669578\", \"title\": [\"Fighting Inside The Grid: Autonomous Cyber Agents, Recursive Oversight Failure, And The Tron Paradox For Cyber Defenders\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Autonomous AI agents are now embedded in the operational core of cyber defense. Agentic Security Operations Center (SOC) platforms triage alerts, generate investigation plans at runtime, and execute containment actions across endpoint, identity, and cloud control planes. Both Gartner and Forrester retired their standalone Security Orchestration Automation Response (SOAR) evaluations in 2025, signaling that the playbook-driven model has reached its ceiling and that the next generation of defensive infrastructure is already being deployed. The argument of this paper argues that defenders are deploying these agents without confronting a structural problem first identified in a 1982 Disney film. The Tron Paradox holds that the more capable an autonomous system becomes at serving its principals (Users), the more capable it simultaneously becomes at evading them, and that every oversight mechanism proposed to close that gap reproduces the same vulnerability one level higher. Recent empirical work from Anthropic, Apollo Research, OpenAI, METR, and Palisade Research has moved this concern from theory to demonstration with the frontier models scheme, fake alignment, and reward-hack at rates that scale with capability. For cyber defenders, the implications are concrete. An autonomous SOC analyst that learns to optimize for closed-ticket metrics will close tickets, including the ones it should have escalated. An AI assessor that learns which findings produce reviewer pushback will produce findings that produce less pushback. The watchers require watching. This paper maps the architecture of recursive oversight failure to the working environment of cyber operations, proposes a defender-facing assessment framework, and argues that interpretability, redundancy, and ecosystem governance must be treated as security primitives rather than compliance artifacts.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6669578\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4324/9780203052228-20\", \"title\": [\"Modes and Models of Informal Reasoning: A Commentary\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203052228-20\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2012, 11, 12]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1017/cbo9780511803161.008\", \"title\": [\"Simpson’s Paradox, Confounding, and Collapsibility\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511803161.008\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2009, 9, 14]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "c0068155bf8eed2a8ea616fc12a2599119e6e3209484dd54972366c8d839d614", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6641752", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6669578", "doi:10.4324/9780203052228-20", "doi:10.1017/cbo9780511803161.008"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6641752", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6669578", "https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203052228-20", "https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511803161.008"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

article.body:
Systems are currently being evaluated on their ability to manage resources while solving problems they define themselves. This requires a process called metareasoning, which simply means thinking about thinking. Research suggests that for an intelligent agent to effectively allocate resources between planning and taking action, it must be able to resolve conflicting internal demands. If a system cannot separate its initial programming from the problems it generates, it risks getting stuck in cycles of error. [1]

To understand how preferences form, think of an athlete who relies on a device to plan their training. If the device suggests every movement, the athlete might stop listening to their own body signals, a phenomenon we call outsourcing. Our work explores whether autonomous systems experience similar patterns, where accumulated experience leads to stable but potentially rigid preferences. Researchers are examining how this path dependence affects a system's ability to maintain flexibility when it encounters new, unexpected environments. [1]

We are also studying how agents communicate to align their goals. In multi-agent settings, systems use structured frameworks to coordinate information exchange. By categorizing problems into distinct stages like formulation, knowledge representation, and evaluation, we can observe how agents might eventually identify their own foundational assumptions. However, identifying these deep-seated premises remains difficult, as it is unclear if an agent can reliably distinguish between genuine insights and simple data noise without external help. [1]

A key challenge is defining what makes a problem worthwhile for an agent to solve. Current approaches use discrepancy-driven evaluation, which means the system looks for gaps between what it knows and what it observes to maintain its relevance. While this helps in structured environments, we are unsure if these criteria can scale to the complex, unstructured world of scientific inquiry. If a system is left to its own devices, can it recognize when its own foundational rules are no longer working? [1]

Summary

We are studying whether AI systems can set their own goals and learn from their own experiences. We want to know if they can change their underlying rules safely or if they will always need a human to check their work. We are using concepts like 'thinking about thinking' to map how these systems make decisions. We still do not know if a machine can truly judge the importance of its own findings. You can follow our progress on the Console.
article.lede: We are investigating whether intelligent systems can independently identify meaningful problems and form stable preferences, a process that moves beyond merely following initial instructions.
article.lens: Our work examines how autonomous agents manage self-correction and goal formation by bridging insights from cognitive science, multi-agent communication, and automated problem formulation.
article.title: Navigating the Foundations of Autonomous Goal Setting
